960197,ca.proc.d.1932-04-13.4.1.1,1932-04-13,,,,stagedirection,,,,On the orders of the day:

Mr. OSCAR L. BOULANGER (Belle-chasse): I would like to direct a question to the Secretary of State (Mr. Cahan). I should like to ask if he has given permission for the use of the Dominion archives building, which belongs to the Canadian people, by the Imperial Order of Daughters of the Empire
Unemployment Orders in Council

for the holding of a reception- in aid of the relief work carried on by the order, at which there will be dancing and bridge playing. I should like to ask also if the minister would condescend to do the same thing for the Native Sons of Canada should they desire to organize a charity ball or bridge party in aid of the civil servants or railway men, for instance, recently dismissed by the government.",,,,

960198,ca.proc.d.1932-04-13.4.2,1932-04-13,8c3c5f1e-ca27-4173-b0cf-e45c76058ebe,ca.m.8768,Hon. C. H. CAHAN (Secretary of State):,Secretary of State of Canada,DAUGHTERS OF THE EMPIRE,,,"I remember that I gave permission for a reception to be held, but whether or not that permission was given the Imperial Order of Daughters of the Empire I am not sure. It was not brought to my attention that there was to be dancing or bridge playing, or any other form of entertainment; I understood it was to be a reception, and I followed the precedent laid down by my predecessors.
If the Native Sons of Canada desire to hold a reception in the same building they should apply in the usual way and I will take the matter into consideration before giving an answer.

960206,ca.proc.d.1932-04-13.6.2,1932-04-13,441e220e-1526-47d2-9b2f-ab5619ae3aac,ca.m.5796,Mr. WILLIAM DUFF (Antigonish-Guys-borough):,,UNEMPLOYMENT ORDERS IN COUNCIL,,,I should like- to direct the attention of the Prime Minister to the suggestion

I made a few days ago that the orders in council which are laid on the table from day to day with regard to unemployment and farm relief moneys be either printed in the votes and proceedings or made an appendix to Hansard. When only one copy is available it is a great inconvenience to members of parliament, and I wondered if the Prime Minister had been able to give the matter consideration and if he had come to a favourable decision.

find they are practically all the same, varying mainly in the amounts for the various provinces to which payments are made, and unless it becomes the general will of the house it is not at the moment regarded as wise that the additional expenditure should be incurred in printing orders in council of that character, which would involve a very large number of pages added either to the votes and proceedings or to the daily copy of Hansard.

Before we proceed with the next order I would like to point out to the hon. member for Antigonish-Guysborough the fact that at page 246 of the votes and proceedings the orders in council tabled yesterday indicate to whom payments are to be made. I think perhaps in the first one the amount is mentioned, $2,000,000, and that succeeding orders in council might be amplified by stating the amount involved; then you would have the name of the province to which payment had been made, and the amount. If that would meet the hon. gentleman's wishes, I might-give directions this afternoon that it be done.

960216,ca.proc.d.1932-04-13.8.1.1.2,1932-04-13,37ffe576-bd7c-473c-af0b-328099234a8c,ca.m.9963,Mr. A. M. EDWARDS (South Waterloo):,,THE BUDGET,CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL,FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE,"Mr. Speaker, may I first of all extend my congratulations to the architeot of this budget, the present Minister of Finance (Mr. Rhodes). While it has in it many tax levies which possibly bear heavily on a certain portion of the community, still I feel that these levies have been placed upon those people best able to pay, and it is to be hoped that ere another year rolls around and another budget has to be prepared better times will prevail which will permit these taxes to foe lowered.

I am not one of those who think that wealth should be conscripted for tax purposes. We depend on the circulation of capital for the development of our industries, and we usually find that those possessing wealth invest it in our industrial establishments. The levying of an excessive income tax seems to me to be a restriction on initiative, for it means that the man who goes out and makes good is penalized until in the higher categories he loses fifty per cent of his income. However, as I said before, perhaps an upturn in business before next session will enable the government to lessen these imposts.

May I say a word to my good friend who preceded me in this debate, the hon. member for South Huron (Mr. McMillan). I have a very great respect for him. For several sessions I have listened to his views on the tariff question, unquestionably they do not change, and I think the hon. member has advanced them so often that he almost believes them himself. I wonder if hon. gentlemen who are constantly advocating a reduction in protection both for business and for industry have ever pictured to themselves what would have happened to this country if we

had not had the tariff protection enacted in the special session of 1930. That measure was taken barely in time. We had the debacle of business in the United States, industrialists there selling their wares for almost anything they could get for them, not on any fair com-i petitive basis by any means. Two years ago I cited an instance, and perhaps it will bear repetition now, with respect ito the heavier lines of goods manufactured in different parts of the United States where freight rates are sufficiently low to offset the long haul, and where they have in operation what is known as a zoning system. The manufacturers of these heavier lines of goods in the New England states have a zone, we will say, as far west as Buffalo; the Buffalo zone extends to Toledo and Detroit; the Toledo and Detroit zone extends as far west as Chicago and Minneapolis, and from those points the zone extends to the Pacific coast. In normal times it is the understanding between those manufacturers that they shall market their goods within itheir respective zones, but when abnormal conditions arise, as was the case in 1930, this understanding is ignored and they have a free hand. The manufacturer of heavy ware in the eastern states will, for instance, market his goods as far west as Minneapolis or Chicago. He is not particular about the price he gets in that zone, but he is particular about the price in his own zone. In other words, he endeavours to hold up the market for his product in bis own zone, and slaughter it in the other zone. Now, what happened on that occasion? Those goods were coming into Canada for a while, but, due to the vigilance of our National Revenue department, their entry was soon stopped. Those goods were valued for duty purposes at the prices at which they were sold in the slaughter zone, so our manufacturers were subjected to most unfair competition, no regard whatever being paid to cost or to distance of distribution; it was simply a matter of keeping their factories going, getting their prices in their own market and slaughtering them in the foreign market. That happened in various lines of industry. If in 1930 we had not taken means to protect ourselves, what would have happened? We would have been faced with an army of 120,000,000 people as against our small army of 10,000,000. As an inevitable result, our market would have been ruined, and there would be no business for our own industries. Therefore I most heartily commend, as do the people whom I have the honour to represent, the action taken by this government in 1930 to protect our home market.

Before I deal with the subject matter of my remarks, I desire to say a word with respect to the suggestion made yesterday by the hon. member for Dufferin-Simcoe (Mr. Rowe), that mixed farming be encouraged by means of a cash bonus. I am not a farmer and do not pretend to know very much about farming, and while I am not giving it as my considered opinion, still I think the proposal is worthy of consideration by the government, and I hope they will deal with it at the proper time.

in normal times amounts to about one hundred thousand. The Textile Journal gives the number of employees in 1927 as 58,937 women on wages and salaries, and 41,497 men in the same category. Prior to 1930, and while the King administration was in office, we had constant adjustments of the tariff; we had for instance, the tariff entirely removed from worsted yarn which was carrying a duty of 12i per cent. One in Sherbrooke and another in Hespeler are two of the largest mills in Canada; they spin the worsted yam from the raw wool and when this tariff was removed, the result was that worsted yarn was brought into this country free of duty and the spinning plants of these mills were closed down. The German people are even offering to sell their machinery to manufacturers in England.

Now just a word about wool. I was very sorry that I was not present when the hon. member for Maple Creek (Mr. Swanston) introduced his resolution on wool. I think I can state pretty clearly the position of the manufacturers in my district, and it is this: I wish to make it clear that the Canadian woollen manufacturers with whom I have talked have raised no objection to a duty being placed on empire wools to protect the Canadian sheep grower provided compensating duties are placed on all customs items covering semi-manufactured or fully manufactured goods made from wool.

The branch of the wool industry which produces the greatest value of manufactures of wool is the knitting industry. The knit goods industry was not protected in 1930 or 1931, and in my opinion duties cannot be placed on wool effectively or without seriously affecting the knitting industry until the French treaty is out of the way and the knitting industry is protected.

In the riding of South Waterloo, which I have the honour to represent in this house, there are two large silk mills. Of course, there are many others in other parts of the country. I wish to take a few minutes of the time of the house to quote from two bulletins issued by the Silk Association of Canada, which very clearly set forth the position of this very important and ever growing industry. The Silk Association of Canada in its bulletin of January 13, 1932 says:

Substantial increase in employment in the full fashioned hosiery mills in Canada in 1931 over 1930 is indicated by comparative production and sales figures now available. For seventeen out of the twenty-one mills in Canada the comparative figures for the nine months ending November, 1931, show an increase of 1,146,600 pairs over the same period in 1930, while the actual figures for hosiery shipped during the same nine months' periods are: 1931, 9,948.360 pairs; 1930, 8,787,156; increase in 1931 over 1930, 1.151,204 pairs. All full-fashioned hosiery now used in Canada is produced in Canada, the imports for the period in review of all classes of silk hosiery, men's and women's, circular and full fashioned, amounted to only 49,392 pairs. As Canada was machined to supply all requirements in normal times, there was no machinery expansion in 1931, present general conditions not warranting any increase.
In its bulletin of January 27, 1932, tihe Silk Association of Canada gives the number of broad silk looms in this country, with the number of yards produced. It says:
Reports from individual mills indicate a substantial increase in production and employment in 1931 over 1930, particularly since last June
when tariff changes were made. The effect of this change is strikingly shown by the import figures of silk fabrics, dyed and finished, for three-month periods during 1931.

Then it gives the figures by quarters, -but as my time is nearly up I will simply say that the importations for 1931 declined steadily in each quarter, with a total importation for 1931 of 5,944,487 yards, valued at $3,031,738.

I listened very -carefully during the debate on unemployment to hear if some solution would be presented that had not already been advanced by the government of Canada, and I heard none. I want to advance this suggestion, -for whatever it may be worth. Prior to seven, eight or nine years ago it was customary for travelling men to go out selling seasonal goods produced in Canada, goods which have always been required in this country. For instance, a man would go out on March 1 to sell underwear, and have his sales completed by May 1. Those goods would be shipped in August or September, and terms of either thirty days less a discount or ninety days net would be given. The result was that the mills had orders, men were engaged, and the financing of operations was carried on under genuine orders. The goods were delivered in the fall and were not paid for until sold. I think that was a very satisfactory way of handling the matter. That condition applied to many lines, particularly those which owing to climatic conditions are required in Canada. That practice is being followed and must be followed in connection with purchases from foreign countries. Why could it not -be carried out in Canada?

We will suppose a man requires fifty dozens of a certain article. He does not necessarily place an order for fifty dozens, but due to his expectation that he will do business equal to the business of the past year, he may place an order for half the quantity. If the half quantity could be secured in the manner I have described I am sure our unemployment situation would be very materially relieved, and with expense to nobody. I offer that suggestion, believing it to be workable. To make it effective extensive educational propaganda would have to be placed in the newspapers. I believe that sustained advertising of any particular line will make it known.

960237,ca.proc.d.1932-04-13.8.1.1.23,1932-04-13,2a8c7330-53c3-44dc-9f77-c16aa6af7898,ca.m.2417,Mr. HENRI BOURASSA (Labelle):,,THE BUDGET,CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL,FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE,Mr. Speaker, will my hon. friend from South Waterloo (Mr. Edwards) excuse me if I do not follow his argument? With a good deal of what he has said I could agree; but the tariff is not the issue now before the house. The Minister of Finance (Mr. Rhodes) has made it quite clear, the government does not
The Budget-Mr. Bourassa
contemplate at this session to express any opinion or offer any tariff policy until after the Imperial economic conference; and in that attitude I think they are right.
I wish to put myself on record candidly and clearly with regard to the three proposals now before us:
by the hon. member for Acadia (Mr. Gardiner), the amendment moved by the hon. member for Shelburne-Yarmouth (Mr. Ralston) and the budget proposals.

With much that the hon. member for Acadia has said I fully agree, especially with his denunciation of the capitalistic system. I am fully convinced, and have been for many years, that that system, as practised throughout the so-called western world, but especially in North America, is bound to bring dire results. War has merely accentuated the evil consequences of that system, and precipitated the issue. But with all due deference, may I say to my hon. friend from Acadia that he has not fully covered the ground. He has truly stated that the so-called capitalistic system has been of very short duration. INoth-ing indeed is more inaccurate than the prevailing opinion that capitalism is the basis of our economic and social fabric. The origin of capitalism, according to the member for Acadia, is the discovery of steam and its application to industry. May I embroaden the statement and say that what has been termed the mechanization of industry is but a material factor which has contributed to the building up of the capitalistic system. To fully understand the problem and its consequences, one has to go further and, as in everything human, to find out the moral and social factors. With my very short studies of economics and sociology I consider the two main sources out of which this system has arisen are to be found in the French revolution and in the doctrines of the Manchester school in England. First, there is the French Jacobinistic theory of unlimited rights of individual property, and then the Manchester advocacy of laisser faire and laisser passer. Applied to the condition described by the hon. member for Acadia, to the mechanization of industry, these two schools of thought have brought the uncontrolled concentration, first of capital, and then of potential wealth in the hands of a few individuals who are practically beyond control. These men, or corporations, have now in their hands, not only the sources of wealth of the masses of the people, but they practically control the sources of credit of the state. When I use the word state I use it in the broadest sense, including federal, provincial and municipal governments.

What has been the result? Within the last twenty or twenty-five years, the irresponsible masters of that system have not only concentrated real wealth and capital sources of production, but they have created artificial wealth. They have created so-called capital and issued paper in the form of stocks, debentures and titles of all sorts, which have no reality. The gullible public have purchased that paper; it has been broadcast, and the masses of the consuming public are paying interest upon false capital and giving to it a value it does not possess.

The credit of the country maintained through the banks and large financial institutions has been lent as a moral-or should I say immoral-support to that fictitious capital. The condition existing in Canada exists on a much larger scale in the United States, and in practically all the countries of the western world. I say now, weighing fully my remarks, that the best incentive which can be given to the doctrines and practices of extreme socialism, even in the form of bolshevism, is not by allowing the distribution of a few pamphlets, or the making of a few silly speeches in some dark corners of the cities of Montreal or Toronto, but by lending the authority of parliament and the government to the maintenance of a system which is just as immoral and anti-social as the system now being practised in Russia.

If this is true1-and I am, and have been convinced for many years that it is-I venture to say that the remedy offered by the hon. member for Acadia is altogether insufficient to cure the evil. Nationalization of currency is a pretty broad expression. In what form it could be practised, or how it could be executed I am not sure; the hon. member has not quite explained. As I understand it he wants the country, through the inflation of money and the control of currency, to pay its debts at an easier rate than the present value of state paper. That might be discussed, though I think it should be discussed internationally. I do not think the situation of Canada or of any other country will be remedied until there is a courageous international understanding to bring down all debts of all countries.

But where I differ still more with the hon. member is in the suggestion that we should have an artificial inflation of money in order to enable people to purchase more. Would it mean purchasing more or simply giving a few more pieces of paper-inflated paper-to purchase the same quantity of goods? I do not see where the people would be better off. I agree much more with the proposal made
The Budget-Mr. Bourassa

last year by the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre (Mr. Woodsworth), that the evil from which we are suffering is not the dearth of wealth or of production but the lack of proper distribution, and I fail to see how by increasing the number of pieces of paper which people accept as the standard of wealth we will foster that better distribution.

Suppose we increase the number of banknotes or government notes, what will it mean? It will mean that if the man who to-day has 100,000 dollar bills, worth perhaps ninety cents, gets double that amount of paper, he will be worth $180,000, nominally. The poor man will double his small amount of money, and the rich man will double his large amount of money; but this will not equalize anything- unless there is some method not contained in the proposal by which we will take from the man who has too much and give to the man who has too little. It may come to that. Certainly, if the so called captains of industry and the chiefs of the large financial institutions do not open their eyes to the situation and come to an understanding with the leaders of state, whether federal, provincial or municipal, and create of their own goodwill and through a sense of the realities, a better distribution of wealth, a time will come-and probably sooner than we expect-when the distribution will be enforced by brutal means. That I do not wish, and for that reason I think it is better to deal with the evil now rather than to shut our eyes to the danger that lies ahead.

Being an old-fashioned man, Mr. Speaker, with a limited knowledge of economics, I think many of the remedies that have been propounded in this and other countries since the war, have one defect: they lack the good old quality of simplicity. I do not think any artificial means, legal or financial, will cure the evils of the world, and our own particular evils, until we all come back to our senses. Public bodies and individuals have more or less lost their heads for the last twenty years. The period of the war, and the short period following it, was a time of intense inebriation. What we need now is to get sober; but not by the old method of taking more gin or whiskey in the morning to cure the headache caused by the intoxication of the preceding evening. At one time that was very much the fashion, but I think that practice has been eliminated by common sense and proper hygiene. What we want is to get sober in the true sense of the word. We must get more economical. People should not be shown a way of spending as much or more money;

they should be shown the way back to common sense by spending less. That is the lesson which should be learned and practised first by governments, by public bodies, by great industrialists and by all men who spend a good deal of money. It should be learned by all classes of people, from the wealthiest to the poorest. We must get back to the point where we live according to our means; and when we get to that point the poor will be entitled to better care by the rich and by public bodies.

The immediate object which this government should have in mind is a reduction in debt and in expenditure. Of course they have to discriminate; of course they have to think of the immediate needs of the people who must be helped; but frankly if the present Minister of Finance (Mr. Rhodes), who is a man of common sense and of judgment, had been given time to look at the figures showing the expenditures of each department of the government and compare them with the expenditures of each department twenty years ago, would he not have found some means of reducing the expenditures of the country to a muoh larger extent, at the same time giving the people who are in dire need what they may require in the way of work, food and clothing?

Then we want a reduction in debts. I am not going to discuss that question at length, because in order to cover the whole issue one would have to consider the international situation. May I simply suggest to the government that they should miss no opportunity in their relations with the British government and with foreign governments, at Geneva and elsewhere, to enhance and foster against all odds and upon all occasions the need of a reduction and even of a cancellation of all war debts? Until that has been done, the world will find no rest, and there is no possibility of an adjustment.

Now, sir, I come to the amendment proposed by the hon. member for Shelburne-Yarmouth (Mr. Ralston). May I say that I read his excellent speech with much interest, particularly the first part of it; but to speak quite frankly, when I came to the end of his remarks and read the amendment I was simply dumbfounded. He gave a broad criticism covering the whole of the budget, with breadth of mind and common sense, and then reduced it all to a small motion confined to the tariff. It seems as if the tariff question has monopolized the minds of a certain number of members in this house; but surely men of broad views, possessing a fair
The Budget-Mr. Bourassa

knowledge of things social, economic and political, ought to realize that in the present state of affairs the tariff is but a small issue in our whole economic problem. Of course, the tariff has to be considered, and I recognize the right of every group and every individual to their own views in that regard; but when the government comes along with a budget which practically does not touch the tariff at all, how can the opposition gain much confidence throughout the country by reducing its policy to a consideration of the tariff?

Possibly it may be said that in his amendment the hon. member condemns the policy of the government in dealing with these matters by order in council. Well and good; but why was not the amendment so framed as to condemn the policy of dealing with all matters by order in council? I offered the opposition that chance last year, when I presented a motion condemning the practice of determining policies by orders in council, especially in relation to the Russian embargo; but, frightened by fits of terror on the part of some of their friends from Quebec because the word ""Russia"" was mentioned, they did not dare vote for a motion condemning in much broader terms the policy adopted by the present government of dealing with these matters by orders in council. In the present amendment the opposition condemns only one policy effected by order in council. I suppose next session they will move another amendment condemning the order in council dealing with insurance companies; two years hence probably they will move another amendment condemning tJhe order in council dealing with bank values, and three years hence they may move still another amendment condemning some other order in council, and so on, until after a decade the people of Canada may be able to find out what is the policy of the Liberal party.

960240,ca.proc.d.1932-04-13.8.1.1.26,1932-04-13,intervention,,,,THE BUDGET,CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL,FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE,Is any comparison meant?

960241,ca.proc.d.1932-04-13.8.1.1.27,1932-04-13,2a8c7330-53c3-44dc-9f77-c16aa6af7898,ca.m.2417,Mr. BOURASSA:,,THE BUDGET,CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL,FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE,All comparisons are

odious. If the task of the government-and I presume they consider it as such-is by their budget to apply to the problems of the next twelve months a fairly safe and makeshift policy in order to collect money enough to pay what they expect to spend, then I think it is a good budget. Taking only the financial aspect, I do not begrudge the Prime Minister all the praise that he deserves in that respect. He has a great capacity in those matters. Of all the public men in Canada to-day he is probably the best financier. And he has proven it in the last twelve months. His followers having empowered him to rule as a dictator, parliament having abdicated to him, I will not say its rights, but its functions and duties, he is undoubtedly the best man to deal with the purely financial aspect of the situation. One of the Prime Minister's followers, in his juvenile enthusiasm, has said that the right hon. gentleman outshines Mussolini. Perhaps next year someone will say that Napoleon Bonaparte is blushing in his tomb at the idea that a much bigger man has succeeded him in the estimation of the world. But, I repeat, all comparisons are odious.

Simply on the matter of finance, authority having been given to the government to meet the situation as they please, I think the Prime Minister has done what he should have done, and has done it well. His order in council to prohibit the export of gold, the moment the government found out what the result would be of the sudden change of policy in Great Britain, was effective. The manner in which he launched and reaped the result of his conversion loan was excellent. I do not share the view of my friend from Shelburne-Yarmouth, that the Prime Minister does not deserve any credit because the people of Canada gave him the money, and will lose by the exchange of their loans. From the purely financial point of view, it was very clever on the part of the Prime Minister to take advantage of a moment of panic, when the people were afraid to risk their money in industry or elsewhere and were gathering up their capital and savings, to invite them to give him that money. So long as the people of Canada and the money investors trust the Prime Minister, it was very clever on his part to hold out his hand and grab their millions at the moment he did-and the treasury has been benefited thereby.
With regard to the national service loan, I am bound to express some little doubt.
The Budget-Mr. Bourassa

When the loan was launched and oversubscribed, the Montreal Gazette-which is one day of the week the organ of the Tory party in Ottawa, another day the organ of the so-called Liberal government in Quebec, and all other days the organ of the Bank of Montreal and high finance-the Montreal Gazette expressed its horror at the idea of the government of Canada accepting $71,000,000 more than what had been asked for. It considered this a breach of faith with the subscribers because the amount asked for was to be limited to S150,000,000 and was for a precise object. Well, although I had no brief from the Prime Minister and his government to plead their case against the Montreal Gazette, next day I came out with an expression of my doubts as to the validity of the criticism of the financial men at the back of the Montreal Gazette. First, I dealt with the object of the loan. All that the prospectus -I have it in my hand-mentioned was that the proceeds of the loan would be used ""to promote the economic and financial welfare of Canada."" There was no limitation, it was just like the carte blanche which parliament gave the Prime Minister. Suppose the Prime Minister had seen fit, for ""the economic and financial welfare of Canada,"" to erect to himself a statue, as did Nebuchadnezzar in years past, he could have spent $50,000,000 of that loan on a golden statue of himself somewhere in this city, and he would have been within the terms of the prospectus. He is to be congratulated on not having abused the carte blanche which was given to him by parliament in this regard as in all others.

But where I think the government went a little beyond the mark was in the use they made of the surplus. Of course, it was sheer nonsense to say that by accepting the $71,000,000 the value of the other $150,000,000 was diminished; ridiculous. There is no such thing as first, second or third mortgages for the various creditors of the government of Canada. All the resources of Canada are pledged to her creditors, whatever piece of paper they may have in their hands or their portfolios. Therefore, I submit the government was not at fault in accepting the oversubscription, but the use they made of it, I think, is matter for fair criticism. In his speech .the other day the Minister of Finance explained that out of the surplus the government advanced $11,600,000 odd to the provinces, and devoted about $41,000,000 to cover deficits of the Canadian National Railways. Well, although nothing was mentioned in the prospectus, I do not believe that anybody who subscribed the $221,000,000 thought the government would make use of any portion of

it to cover a part of the deficits of the Canadian National Railways so as to enable them to bring down a better budget. I will come back to that in a moment. It was centainly not contemplated, it was not mentioned, and I believe the sooner the government .take steps to apply the whole of the $221,000,000 in reducing the outstanding debt of the country, or rather in substituting these new securities for the old securities that may become due before long, the closer they will be .to carrying out their moral obligation towards the people of Canada.

With regard to the advances to the provinces, I have no hesitation in saying that the federal government only did what it had to do. I am not referring to the amounts or to the manner in which they were paid, I refer only to the basic principle that the government of Canada, being responsible for the credit of Canada as a whole, has not only -the right but the duty to see that no public, body in Canada goes by default and thereby creates a feeling in the financial world which will react against the credit of the government of Canada. So, in that respect I think the government did right. On the other hand, I do not agree absolutely with the view expressed the other day by the hon. member for North Winnipeg (Mr. Heaps) in connection with the observations of the hon. member for Shelburne-Yarmouth (Mr. Ralston) in this regard. I do not think the criticism of the hon. member for Shelburne-Yarmouth warranted the comment that he was merely raising a technicality against these advances. The government did what it should have done, and what it may have to do again in the future, in coming to the rescue of the provinces; but surely some basis must be arrived at whereby the provinces and the government respectively would not foe in the position of bankrupt clients at the mercy of their banker. As I understood the hon. member for Shelburne-Yarmouth, that was his contention, and in that respect I fully agree.

,Conservative (1867-1942),,Edgar Nelson Rhodes,http://www.parl.gc.ca/parlinfo/Files/Parliamentarian.aspx?Item=0ad88e35-0ebb-4dd8-9601-b39a599b36d1&Language=E&Section=ALL
960249,ca.proc.d.1932-04-13.8.1.1.35,1932-04-13,2a8c7330-53c3-44dc-9f77-c16aa6af7898,ca.m.2417,Mr. BOURASSA:,,THE BUDGET,CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL,FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE,Quite so, but there is

something much more important than that. The duty of the government is not merely to make matters more or less right for twelve months. It has undertaken the obligation of providing some remedy, some permanent remedy for the situation now confronting Canada. Then I say that the matter of finance, important as it is, concerns only a small portion of the situation.

It may be considered to be a hobby of mine; but I have long advocated the necessity of a complete recasting of our taxation system. This system has grown up haphazardly through the various changes in government and the necessities of the times; but since the war, and largely on account of the war, the economic, social and financial condition of the world has been so completely altered as to make it impossible to maintain unaltered the old systems of finance and administration. I do not contend that these systems should be discarded entirely, but I do say that a deep study of these matters should be made by thinking men, irrespective of party and political creeds in matters of trade or tariffs, in order to find some basis of taxation which will result in bettering conditions for the people of Canada. It has been written of late, and I think quite rightly, that perhaps the greatest administrator in England during the last two centuries was Robert Walpole. This man's name was long a matter of obloquy, his reputation was much discussed; but in my opinion, in matters economic, he rendered better service to Great Britain than any other man. The permanent results of his policy were brought about because of the fact that in all matters of taxation and finance he endeavoured to arrive at a proper apportionment of sources of profit and of state burdens as between the different classes of the community. He was not a man of the city, he was a man of the country; he was not an instrument of the tradesmen, the agriculturists or the industrialists; he wanted to make

matters such that all classes should derive a proper share of benefits and contribute a proper share of support to the maintenance of their country. I think the same thing might be said, although to a lesser degree, of Mr. Gladstone as a chancellor of the exchequer.

In connection with the income tax, I approve heartily of the reductions made in the exemptions. On the whole the proposals of the government are far in advance of those of last year. Nevertheless, I suggest, as I have suggested to predecessors of the minister, that in order to give social and economic justice, there should be a sharp difference as between salaries earned from year to year and income derived from invested capital. Proper means should also be taken to prevent debenture holders from defrauding the state as they have been doing ever since the income tax was established. These people do not declare their coupons because they are paid through the banks. I was told repeatedly by the late Mr. Leroux of Montreal, a gentleman who gave excellent service to the crown, that he was convinced the government had lost millions of dollars in the case of his own office alone. I have been told also by different accountants in Montreal, the most respected men in their profession, that estates with incomes of between $20,000 to $30,000 have not paid one cent of income tax for years, because all their holdings being invested in debentures payable to bearer, no declarations have been made, and no trace left of the evasions. In the past, I have suggested the affixing of a stamp to the coupons, as is done in England; but I have come to the conclusion that this would not be sufficient; the holders of large quantities of debentures would pay simply so much per hundred instead of paying on a sliding scale. The only way to handle these debentures is to adopt the method used in the case of stocks; force the debenture holders to inscribe their debentures, and then force the company to give a yearly report of the debentures inscribed, just as is done in the case of dividends paid on stocks. In this way the government could reach the debenture holder as it reaches the shareholder.

I come now to the excise tax. Why should not the government call this tax by its true name and term it a special customs duty? It is not an excise tax, it is a customs duty levied over and above the ordinary rates established by the customs tariff.
With regard to the sales tax, I claim, without discussing the rate now, because I have no time, that the tax should be levied at the
The Budget-Mr. Bourassa

end and not at the root; in other words, that it should be paid by the consumer when he purchases his needs instead of being charged to the manufacturer or the wholesale merchant. Under the present system the people do not know what proportion they pay to the government, what to the retailer, what to the wholesaler and what to the middleman. My authority for making this suggestion to the government is one which I think will commend itself to members on the other side of the house, that of their own Prime Minister when, sitting on this side, he stated emphatically that one of the essential things connected with taxation is that it should be visible. This kind of invisible taxation which enables a series of intermediaries to pile up profits, dividends and interest upon the sales tax they have paid to the government, is wrong. The government does not get the whole amount and the ratepayers do not realize what they are paying.

I shall not dwell upon the question of trade. I am glad, however, the hon. member for Shelburne-Yarmouth once more pricked that old bubble, a ""'favourable balance of trade."" I well remember in the old days, disputes, discourses and debates between the two parties, the two main speakers of which were then Sir Richard Cartwright and Sir George Foster. How many illustrations and counter-examples I have heard about the favourable balance of trade! To reduce the question to an argument ad absurdum which should appeal to the common sense of the Minister of Finance, supposing by your trade policy, or as a result of existing conditions, all the imports of Canada were reduced to S500 and our exports reached the high sum of SI,000. Of course, you would have a favourable balance of trade of 100 per cent over your imports; but where would the Canadian people be? Undoubtedly, these things are very complex. I well remember the great fight in England on Mr. Chamberlain's proposals for trade reform. The strongest argument made against his reasoning about the decline in the trade balance was that of Mr. Asquith, regarding the amount of invisible trade, for example, the value of the shipbuilding industry and of the shipping trade, which were not tabulated in trade returns, but which meant to the people of England much more than the difference between imports and exports. I am giving that simply as an example to show that this shibboleth of favourable balance of trade does not mean much. What counts, after all, is what every man is capable of selling, what he gets for what he sells, what he is capable of
purchasing, and what he pays for his purchases.

In closing may I say that if the budget is looked upon as a balance sheet of a private corporation, then it is a fairly well balanced sheet-with this little difference between a private concern and the government, that the Minister of Finance will endeavour, by taxing the people of Canada, to make good the deficit. Of course he does not expect that with this new taxation he will overcome his deficit next year; he knows he will not, and it would be far better to let the people of Canada know this. I suppose, as we do with children, he wants to give the medicine by doses, but I do not believe in deceit. It is just as well to tell the Canadian people that we are in for a few more black years; that they must prepare to pay more and to be more in debt, and therefore they must economize, economize and economize. The government and all the public and financial bodies should show them an example in this regard. It is no use buoying up the people with false hopes-

960254,ca.proc.d.1932-04-13.8.1.1.40,1932-04-13,2383d6a2-7bc8-4d50-94b0-288e425fa899,ca.m.4026,Mr. HOWARD:,,THE BUDGET,CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL,FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE,That is the argument which is usually put up in the house, and I should like to make this statement frankly: I cannot see what that has to do with Canadians. What I am interested in is the position of the people of Canada.

In passing, may I make this suggestion to the Minister of Finance, and I am sure in his fairmindedness he will accept it; when he presents his next budget twelve months from now, I would appreciate it very much if he would have it translated and presented to the house in both languages at the same time. There are many French newspapers throughout the country and it is a great hardship to them to have to translate the budget and publish it at the same time as it appears in English newspapers.
I remember sitting in the house last year when the former Minister of Finance, the present Prime Minister (Mr. Bennett), presented 'his budget. As reported on page 2168 of Hansard of 1931, he said:
I shall come first of all to a statement of anticipated revenues and expenditures. I will admit that this is the first time for many years that this country has had a budget.

Then he estimated the revenues at $410,000,000, and he estimated that there would be a deficit of $7,000,000 in the operations for the past twelve months. Now for that period for which the former Minister of Finance estimated there would be a deficit of $7,000,000 we actually had a deficit of $119,000,000. In other words, the former Minister of Finance was $112,000,000 out in his calculations for those twelve months, and that is some difference.

The hon. Minister of Trade and Commerce (Mr. Stevens) criticized very severely the manner of presentation of former budgets. May I say to him in passing that in comparing the two administrations, we want the Liberal government to be judged on performance, and I am sure that the present government will have to be judged on its promises. In presenting the budget the other day the Minister of Finance on page 1751 of Hansard gave a summary of all revenues for five-year periods. I shall take only the figures for the last year of the Liberal administration, as given by the Minister of Finance. The revenues in 1930 amounted to $446,000,000, and during the past year they dropped to $334,000,000, or a decrease of nearly $112,000,000 under the present government as compared with the last year under the former administration. Against those revenues, according to this same table supplied by the Minister of Finance, the expenditures during the last year of the late Liberal administration were $398,000,000, and last year the expenditures under the present government were $454,000,000, or an increase in expenditure of almost $56,000,000, plus a declining revenue of $112,000,000.
directors of a corporation whose business manager presented any such statement as that to the board, I leave it to the judgment of the house to say what would happen to him.

Dealing as concisely as I can with some other figures which I wish to give to the house, the estimated taxation revenue for this year is $273,000,000, and with the tax increases proposed that amount should be raised to $319,000,000. The Finance minister estimates that at the end of this year's operations he will have a surplus of $4,300,000. Well, all I can say with regard to that estimate is that I hope the year's operations will come nearer to the estimate than was the case with the estimate of the former Minister of Finance.

I do not wish to criticize the budget in detail, but there are a few comments which I wish to make before taking it up in another way. First a word as to the sales tax. The Business Week of March 16, 1932, commenting on the sales tax, says:

Heavy sales taxation is a stigma that attaches to the fiscal system of every backward and benighted nation, and is an underlying cause of their backwardness because it retards business expansion and the development of new industries.

If, as some hon. gentlemen opposite suggest, the sales tax is to be passed on to the consumer, then it immediately becomes a poor man's income tax. Take the case of two men, one with an income of three thousand dollars and the other with an income of ten thousand dollars. The house must realize that regardless of what a person's income is, almost any two people will consume about the same
The Budget-Mr. Howard

amount of certain commodities-soap, for instance. The sales tax on soap will therefore represent a greater percentage of the three thousand dollar income than of the ten thousand dollar income. On the other hand, some hon. gentlemen may say that the manufacturer will absorb the tax. Let me give an illustration in that connection. In the city of Sherbrooke a certain manufacturer is producing a product which sells in the markets of the world to the amount of $100,000. In an adjoining city another manufacturer is producing a product which sells to the amount of $100,000. Each of these manufacturers pays $6,000 into the treasury under this proposed taxation, but if one manufacturer has a profit of $15,000 on his turnover, and the other a profit of $20,000, it means that the man with the less profit will pay 40 per cent as compared with the other man's 15 per cent, and that I say is unfair.

I notice that the stamp tax on cheques has been raised to six cents on every cheque over $10.0. I cannot see that that will make much difference because during the last year and a half the cheques drawn in my constituency for over $100 were very much fewer than they used to be.

But if we are to accept the budget as the inevitable consequence of the government's policies in the past, I appeal to the government now to say what their policies are going to be in the future to remedy the situation in this country within the next twelve months. What is their policy to be in connection with industry during the next twelve months? What is their policy to be in connection with agriculture, and every member of the house knows the deplorable condition of agriculture in this country? What is their policy to be in connection with unemployment? What is their policy to be in connection with finance? What is their policy to be in connection with trade? If this budget is to be imposed upon the people and the people are to be called upon to deny themselves to meet this increased taxation, we have a right to know what the government policies will be upon the five subjects that I have just enumerated.

Touching for a moment on the trade figures, I find that in 1930, the last year of the Liberal administration, the total foreign trade of Canada, imports and exports combined, was $2,393,000,000. One year later, in 1931, that figure had shrunk to $1,723,000,000, and for the year ending March 31, 1932, the figure had shrunk still further to $1,168,000,000, or less than fifty per cent of what the trade of this country was when the Liberal government went out of power. I attribute a great deal of that shrink-

age in the trade of this country to the tariff policies of this government, and again I ask the government, what is their tariff policy going to be in the next twelve months, so that industry and agriculture and labour will know what is going to happen to them. I notice that in making these remarks I am in agreement with the present Minister of Railways and Canals (Mr. Manion) who, at page 2836 of Hansard of April 20, 192:6, condemned the government of that day because they had made tariff changes without first referring them to a tariff board for consideration, and he moved an amendment which concluded with these words:
And this house regrets that in the case of drastic changes announced in the budget such assurances-
That is, assurances to refer the proposed changes to the tariff board:
-have not been fulfilled.
I ask him this question:
twelve months how have the changes in the tariff been made? When I ask for a statement of the policy of the present government,

I must refer to the remarks of the hon. member for Labelle (Mr. Bourassa) who said that these changes should be decried by everybody because they were not made on business principles. I believe those changes were made in the manner described by the hon. member for Shelburne-Yarmouth, because of pressure in certain places by certain manufacturers who either were or were not friends of the government. The changes in the tariff which have been made by order in council I would call grasshopper tariff regulations, and I make that classification advisedly. After all, if there is one thing which requires stability, certainly that thing is the changing of the tariff. A man wants to know what the present tariff on an article is, and what it is going to be. After he has shipped the goods he does not want to learn that the rate has been changed to such an extent that he cannot enter the market.

The two greatest problems before Canada to-day are those concerning our railways and the deepening of the St. Lawrence river. Neither of these matters has been submitted ' to the house during this session, and the subjects which have been brought up for discussion, and most of the bills considered, have been of very little interest to Canada. Certainly their importance is small when we compare them with the outstanding questions we should consider. I should like to draw to the attention of hon. members the position,
The Budget-Mr. Howard

as I see it, of labour, agriculture and finance. Two years ago government financing was done at an interest rate of only four and one-half per cent. At that time labourers were receiving about forty cents an hour, and receipts for agricultural products were on a fairly profitable basis. What is the position to-day? I think the conditions obtaining in this particular connection are more serious than any other phase of the problem. The rates of interest on government financing have increased to five per cent, six per cent and six and cne-quarter per cent. Wages have gone below twenty cents an hour, and the prices for agricultural products are lower than they have been during the past twenty-five years. This condition of affairs cannot continue. The rate of interest on money cannot be maintained by depreciating the wages paid to labour and the prices of agricultural products. The rates of interest must come down to a reasonable basis; wages must go up, and there must be fair receipts on the sale of agricultural products, if we are to maintain a business equilibrium in Canada.

I shall now direct my remarks to the question of unemployment, and appeal to the government to proclaim their policy for the next twelve months. I do not like to repeat the promises made, but I am tempted to quote the words of the Prime Minister at Regina on June 12, 1930:
This is a new country, and there is no excuse for unemployment in Canada if a government does its duty.
Speaking in Moncton on July 10, he said:

The Conservative party is going to find work for all who are willing to work, or perish in the attempt, and take such steps as will end this tragic condition of unemployment and bring prosperity to the country as a whole.
Month-Year
October, 1931
And then this further appeal was made to the electors.
Mr. King promises consideration of the problem of unemployment; I promise to end unemployment. Which plan do you like best?

For the information of hon. members I should like to present some figures concerning unemployment. I have (before me a list of unemployment statistics for about twenty countries. These figures, which are for the last twelve months, show that Great Britain is second from the 'bottom, unemployment in that country having increased only 12 per cent. Canada, however, is fifth from the top, unemployment having increased (by 80 per cent. I have before me a letter from the secretary-treasurer of the city of Sherbrooke comparing the unemployment situation of 1931 with that of 1932. The total number of unemployed in Sherbrooke in 1931 was 1,201; today it is 1,812.

I should like to outline the assistance given to the unemployed in the city of Sherbrooke. Possibly the facts I am about to, disclose will indicate at least one reason why agricultural products are selling at such a low level. Single men are allowed to work one day per week at 25 cents an hour for an eight hour day, yielding $2, on which they must subsist. Married men without children receive two days work each week at the same rate, yielding .$4; married men with families work three days a week at the same rate, and receive $6. The total number of unemployed who got employment from the city in the year 1931 was 945; this year on February 24, 1,614 were receiving employment.

In the city of Sherbrooke we supply those without funds with free wood, and I should like to run over a few of the figures in this connection. I shall place on Hansard the following record of delivery of wood:
Month-Year
October, 1930
This shows the situation as to unemployment relief. I suggest when the government asks for increased taxation, at least it should tell the house its policy in connection with unemployment relief.

I should like to tell hon. members something about the industrial situation in Sherbrooke. A few days ago the Prime Minister referred to the silk industry of that city, and made the statement that that industry was in a prosperous condition. We have two silk

industries in Sherbrooke which produce 60 per cent of all the full-fashioned silk hosiery' manufactured in Canada, or ten per cent more than half. Those industries are fairly prosperous, although I shall give some figures in a few moments which may indicate that during the past year sales have been much lower. The profit is lower than it was previously, the 3 per cent excise on the raw material, the ten per cent depreciation in currency, the eleven per cent profit tax, and
The Budget-Mr. Howard
the six per cent sales tax will be detrimental to those industries. I am waiting to learn the result of next year's operations.

Our specialty steel manufacturers, which used to employ 75 hands, now employ only 15. This year those employees are working only 28 hours per week as against 35 last year. There is a wage reduction of ten per cent and the foundry is closed entirely. Further, I shall relate the conditions in connection with our largest steel manufacturing industry. The pay-roll to-day shows 200 or 300 men less than it did at peak periods, and in that large industry the foundry is closed alternate weeks. This year the plant is operating only four days per week, while last year it operated five.

One of our textile industries has dropped twelve employees; they are paying $500 per week less wages, and the value of their product has dropped 40 per cent. Another textile industry which formerly employed 1,500 hands employs now only 200 or 300, some of which work two days and others three days per week. Only a few work the full week. Another industry reports that business has dropped 40 per cent during the last year; it has reduced the number of its employees 20 per cent, and is working four days a week as compared with five and a half days last year. Another steel industry states its profits this year are much less than they were last year; they are working one hour less per day and the number of employees has been reduced by ten per cent. Here is a rubber industry doing only one-half the business of last year, with wages 15 per cent less and the number of employees reduced by 10 per cent. Here is another steel industry; whose volume of business this year is only one-sixth what it was last year; wages are down 25 per cent; the number of employees has been reduced 40 per cent and they are working a seven-hour day and a five-day week as against a ten-hour day and six-day week last year. Another steel industry which ordinarily employs about 150 men last year employed about 80, and I consulted the manager of that company last Friday and found that the company was now employing only 7 men. Consider what that means, with the overhead and everything else, and only 7 employees working. It means the company will have to draw on its surplus, dividends will be passed and so on; it also means no work for the labouring men and no wages with which to pay the bills of their families.

I was surprised to learn the facts connected with another manufacturing concern in Sherbrooke. It went out of business two weeks ago, loaded all its machinery on freight cars and shipped it back to the United States.

Formerly this concern employed 40 hands, but it will do no more business in Canada. Last year our Sherbrooke street railway suspended operations. I am not trying to find fault with my own town, but I do wish to place before this government the gravity of the situation, and to appeal to them again to tell us what they are going to do to settle the unemployment problem, what they intend to do for industry, and what they are going to do for our trade, because if we have no trade we will have no labour and no industries in this country.

I should like to give just one more outstanding example of what this grasshopper tariff legislation can do for a country. In the budget presented last year by the right hon. Prime Minister a one per cent excise tax was imposed on all imports, including lumber. It must be remembered that a very small quantity of lumber comes into Canada in comparison with the enormous quantity of lumber we export to the United States, but the one per cent excise tax was applied, and what happened? In the United States tariff law there is a provision, which I will not read, that if Canada, for instance, applies a duty against United States lumber, that country will apply a duty of $1 per thousand feet against lumber entering the United States from Canada. That stopped shipments of Canadian lumber to the United States. It did not take long to get some action; delegations stormed Ottawa, and the then Minister of Finance saw that a serious mistake had been made. By order in council, again, he amended the tariff and took off the one per cent excise tax on lumber. The Prime Minister was trying to blast his way into the markets of the world; this was one of his experiments. Uncle Sam was not satisfied with that action, however; he said, ""That is a very good order in council, but I am sorry we will still have to apply the duty of $1 against Canadian lumber."" Then what happened? This government had to pass another order in council making that regulation retroactive, so that it was as though the one per cent tax had never applied to lumber, and they had to refund all the money collected up to that time. That demonstrates the extraordinary habit of this government of changing duties, applying taxes and granting exemptions without due consideration.
Before I leave the question of industry there is another point with which I should like to deal. At page 54 of Hansard the Prime Minister is reported as having said:
Incidentally to the discharge of these obligations we have improved employment in Canada.
The Budget-Mr. Howard
I am not going to answer that statement, but I cannot understand 'how it could have been made. The Prime Minister then said:
There are a hundred more industries in this country than there were when the present government came into power.
The hon. member for South Waterloo (Mr. Edwards) said there were 157 new industries, and yesterday the hon. member for Dufferin-Simcoe (Mr. Rowe) said there were 142 What are the facts?

knows, and the hon. member for Stanstead (Mr. Hackett) knows, that before making a statement of that kind consideration should be given t'he number of factories which have closed their doors. As a matter of fact, during the period in which one hundred new industries came to Canada, 464 industries closed their doors.

Now I wish to touch on agriculture. This question does not affect the county of Sherbrooke so greatly, but it will have to be dealt with by my hon. friend from Compton (Mr. Gobeil), my hon. friend from Stanstead (Mr. Hackett), my hon. friend from Brome-Missisquoi (Mr. Pickel) and my hon. friend from Shefford (Mr. Tetreault) when the timp comes. I would like to have time to compare some of the ministers of agriculture of the past with the present minister, but I never deal with .personalities. I will only say that the Minister of Agriculture (Mr. Weir) from his place in this house called an hon. member on this side a back bencher. I want to say to the minister that the only difference between himself and a back bencher is that a back ibencher is a future .cabinet minister who has not lost touch with the common people.

This week, coming through the city of Montreal, I learned to my surprise that the new price for milk, which will be announced on April 15, will be $1.35 per hundred pounds delivered in Montreal. If you take off 35 cents a hundred for express it means that $1 per hundred will be paid for milk delivered in Montreal. I do not want to criticize those engaged in the milk business in that city; I know something about that business, but they will sell it at $4 per hundred. If this government were alive to the situation surely they could at least reduce the price of milk to the consumer or, 'better still, increase the price to the farmer, and God knows he needs it.
In going over the estimates this year and noticing the way they 'have been curtailed

I marvelled that the ministers of the crown, knowing the condition of agriculture, should have consented to the reduction of the agricultural estimates by some $3,000,000. I do not criticize the idea of lessening our expenditures, but if there is one place where under present conditions this government has no right to curtail expenditures it is in connection with the agriculture of Canada. I would ask the members from the eastern townships what they are going to do with regard to the Sherbrooke exhibition, which up to this year has been granted $5,000 yearly by the Dominion government. That money does not go into the treasury of the Sherbrooke fair; it represents one-third of the amount paid directly to the farmers in that part of the .country. Now this government have cut off that grant; in other words they have refused to pay one-third of the prize money given the farmers of the eastern townships. What did the Quebec government do? They are just as hard up as this government is and their situation is just as bad. But the Quebec government are paying two-thirds, or $10,000, to the Sherbrooke fair. Although this government has gone 'back on agriculture in the eastern townships, the Quebec government are paying their $10,000 just the same, and they have also given $2,500 to apply on the deficit of last year.

May I, Mr. Speaker, place upon Hansard certain comparative figures with regard to prices of farm products. Each year I have watched this situation, and I have before me the prices for February 15, 1930, February 15, 1931, and yesterday's prices. These are taken from the Montreal Gazette. In 1930 eggs sold at 50 cents a dozen. That is what the farmers in the eastern townships were getting when the Mackenzie King government was in power. In 1931 eggs sold at 30 cents a dozen. Yesterday the price of eggs was 22 cents, in fact, some extras were sold at 19 cents. In 1930 butter fat sold at 42 cents a pound; in 1931 at 33 cents a pound; and yesterday at 21 cents. Fluid milk brought 7 cents a quart in 1930, 5 cents in 1931, and 4 cents yesterday. Butter was selling at 37 cents a pound in 1930, and the farmers were fooled and voted against the King administration because the price dropped 5 cents a pound at that time, but last year the price receded to 30 cents a pound, and yesterday it was only 17 cents a pound. This week farmers' butter was selling at 10 cents a pound in Lennoxville. Live stock prices have dropped in the same proportion.
Does the Minister of Finance realize the situation in which our eastern township farmers find themselves to-day? Any farmer who has
The Budget-Mr. Howard

no mortgage interest to meet and food in his cellar can at least get three meals a day, but the farmer whose land is encumbered cannot meet even his interest payments. Within the last two months two farmers who had put all their money into their farms and were financially embarrassed saw their property sold over their heads to speculators, and those speculators have since come to this government to ask assistance under the farm loan credit legislation.

A few minutes ago the hon, member for Labelle (Mr. Bourassa) said the Prime Minister is supposed to be an expert in finance. If I had time I should like to talk about the financing that has been done by this government during the past two years. Take the conversion loan. It is true our people came across with their money. But, as member for the county of Sherbrooke, I feel a terrible responsibility, because men of that county came to me and said, ""We are invited to convert our victory bonds. Do you think, Mr. Howard, we should do so V' I am proud of the answer I gave them, but, Mr. Speaker, I am sorry for the results. But, the results would have been different if we had not had a change of government. I told those men, ""If the government want you to convert your bonds I think you should do so."" They converted their bonds. What happened? Insiders of this government did not convert their bonds; the people of Sherbrooke and the eastern townships did. To-day their bonds are selling at 92, and the bonds that those insiders did not convert are selling at 104. When I look around and see the lack of confidence, the financial hysteria that has overcome this country, I am appalled. I stand here as a business man, and if I could do anything to inspire confidence in our people I would do so. I think we have the best banking system in the world, but the banks of Canada and this government are one, they are working together. Surely they could work together in such a way as to show better results.

W OODS WORTH (Winnipeg North Centre):,,THE BUDGET,CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL,FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE,Mr. Speaker, I must congratulate the Minister of Finance (Mr. Rhodes) on the clarity and comprehensiveness of his statement. He began with a review of the events which have so profoundly influenced international finance and reacted on our own stiuation. In that review he asserted:
The world is close knit to-day in matters of trade and finance as never before in history . . . and we cannot expect normal or prosperous conditions apart from the general world trend.

I agree heartily with this statement, and, so far as I can recall, it is the best we have had on our international relationships. But I could have wished that the Minister of Finance had gone a little bit further and offered some definite course of action which would have helped to promote some sort of international solution. The budget does not indicate any international cooperation whatever. Let me give one or two illustrations as to how this lack may affect us. Out in the west all our agricultural arrangements are built up on the principle of a large export crop. Within the last few years the export markets have been very largely closed. So far as I can see the situation, there is no future for western agriculture unless the markets in Europe, or possibly in the orient, are open, and yet there is no indication whatever that the government is taking any steps through which we might hope for an opening-up of markets for western wheat.

Moreover, the tariff arrangements, in the last few months have been such as to make more difficult the selling of our goods abroad. Doctor Marvin, an economist of the Royal bank, in a recent address before the Canadian club of Toronto, as reported in the Financial Times of February 26, said:
Tariff barriers have hindered the free interchange of goods, and the recent increases in tariffs are more than likely to delay recovery.

I presume Doctor Marvin was speaking of world tariffs, but what is true of tariffs in Europe is equally true of tariffs on this continent. There is no indication that our own government is giving any lead in the direction of lowering those tariffs and thus making possible a greater measure of international cooperation.

I was very glad to hear the Minister of Trade and Commerce (Mr. Stevens) deal with the question of finance. Up to a very short time ago we in this comer had very little support when we mentioned matters of finance.

I am hoping that before very long the minister will get a little further than to think that if we have bimetalism we shall have solved our problems. He did, however, advance some very sound propositions. In this connection I would quote a further extract from Doctor Marvin's address:

The price level depends upon the ratio of credit and production. When credit expands excessively prices rise, and when credit is unduly contracted prices fall . . . volume of credit has fallen faster than volume of production ... it is this relationship which has produced falling prices. . . . There cannot be a return to the price level of 1926-28 unless credit
The Budget-Mr. Woodsworth
expansion is more rapid than increase in production, and a return to that price level is essential if the world's load of indebtedness is to be tolerable.

I am not very much concerned in keeping the world's indebtedness as it is, but I would point out that unless it is made tolerable, the present system is in danger of eminent collapse. Although the government presumably is in favour of maintaining the present system, it is taking no steps to ensure that it will extend even for a comparatively limited period.

Let us consider our rigid adherence to gold as the basis of currency and credit. In his very admirable review the Minister of Finance (Mr. Rhodes) said that gold was ceasing to be a medium of exchange and was becoming instead a commodity to be jealously guarded. If that is true, I cannot for the life of me understand why the Minister of Finance should not take steps to get away from the gold standard. If gold is ceasing to perform its primary function, that is, to permit the exchange of goods, why should we continue to use it as the basis of our medium of exchange? Why not select some other- medium which would enable us to perform the task of effecting exchange? However, if the minister is determined to cling to the gold standard, then I have a suggestion to make. Why not expropriate the gold mines of this country and enlist an army of unemployed -to work those mines to the very limit? If gold is to be the basis of our credit system and if the recovery of prosperity of this country is to depend upon the increase in gold, then let us work our gold mines and get things started. Instead of doing that, we are passing over to private individuals whatever profits may be made out of gold. Apparently we cannot produce sufficient gold to form a basis upon which our credit can be extended and prosperity brought back.

There is an incidental matter to which I shall refer for a moment. The revenue from public services is given as $54,000,000, the greater part being from the post office, which shows an increase of $1,500,000. Since this is true, I suggest that in these times of depression we attempt to give public ownership a chance and extend public service into other fields. The government is expected to carry on non-profit bearing enterprises and leave the profit-bearing to private individuals. Coming down on the train I was talking to a gentleman about the output of the briquetting plant near Estevan. I understand that this is a fairly remunerative proposition, it being now in the hands of an American company. Hon. members who have been in the house for some years will remember that large sums of money were paid out for experimental work in the development of that briquetting plant. I do not see why, when we develop an enterprise of this kind, we cannot hold on to it and make it produce revenue for the country and give service to the people rather than turn it over to a private concern.

The Minister of Finance was able to report that he had balanced the budget so far as current services were concerned, but I ask: What has been the cost to the countiy as a whole for this balancing of the budget? I venture to say that the minister's method of balancing has made it more difficult for the majority of the people to balance their own private budgets. There has been a lessening of income because of increased taxation and an increase in other costs because of customs duties and so on. Although this problem may have been settled from the standpoint of the minister, it means that most of us will have difficulty in balancing our own budgets.
This balancing has been effected in two ways, by a reduction in expenditure, that is, by the cutting down of staffs, salaries and
The Budget-Mr. Woodsworth

services, and by increased taxation. I suggest respectfully to the Minister of Finance that there are other ways in which the budget might have been balanced. It might have been balanced by increasing the taxes on great wealth, it might have been balanced by the cutting down of debts, or it might have been balanced by the concurrent application of both methods.

The minister referred to uncontrollable expenditures which include debt charges, pensions, ex-soldier welfare work, provincial subsidies and other writings, aggregating altogether $236,000,000, or 62 per cent of the total debt. I always object to the word ""uncontrollable,"" I do not like to think that bondholders are in a class by themselves and that we cannot touch anything which concerns them. Let me point out to the house that the real value of these debts has practically doubled since they were contracted. We heard a great deal this afternoon from the hon. member for South Waterloo (Mr. Edwards) about cloth. Supposing he contracted to deliver one hundred yards of cloth; the yardstick is three feet in length but if in some mysterious way that yardstick was stretched to six feet, I wonder if he would like to have to fulfil his contract and deliver one hundred yards of six feet each. That is precisely what we are asked to do with regard to our debts. There has been a contraction of credit, price levels have fallen and the purchasing power of the dollar to-day is practically twice what it was when these debts were contracted. We are continuing to pay interest on bonds based on their face value, and that seems to me to be absolutely unjustifiable ethically. The hon. member for Labelle (Mr. Bourassa) a few moments ago was speaking of the iniquity of paying dividends on watered stock, but it seems to me to be equally iniquitous to ask this country to pay interest on the the face value of bonds when their real value has doubled since the time they were issued.

government makes a charge of that kind, we ought to have some statement with regard to the matter. I think we all do know something about a later transaction than that in connection with the .provincial savings bank of Manitoba, which was forced to close its doors a few weeks ago. We do know that Mr. Bracken, the premier of the province of Manitoba, appealed to the Prime Minister of Canada for help, and at first it was refused. Later, after some negotiations, the Prime Minister took the matter into his consideration, and finally on February 9 he wired to Premier Bracken:
You will be advised by code telegram to-morrow the terms on which your proposals will be accepted.
There came no further word from the Prime Minister. The next communication to Mr. Bracken was from the banks, a telegram dated February 11, which reads in part as follows:

Referring to your previous conversations with bankers and also with the Prime Minister of Canada and the Prime Minister's message to you last night, banks represented in Winnipeg are willing to assume deposit liabilities if you address a communication in the following terms to them.

Here is a message from the private banks to a provincial government saying that ""if you address a communication in the following terms to them,"" then there followed a number of definite conditions, among which I find the following:
The government of the province of Manitoba will within a period not exceeding fourteen days from the date hereof convene the legislature and repeal said chapter 174 and amendments thereto.

That is I believe the statute providing for the establishment of a provincial savings bank in Manitoba. Premier Bracken protested against some of the conditions dictated to him by the banks. Negotiations went on for a little time and the banks finally consented to his plea that .the legislation should not be repealed, but Premier Bracken agreed that the government would not again go into savings bank business. Finally we have this from the banks:
Referring your message of Saturday, have consulted banks, who are agreeable to waiving the repeal feature provided legislature is convened within two weeks from to-morrow.
There you have private banks indicating how this country is to be governed.
