960273,ca.proc.d.1932-04-13.8.1.1.59,1932-04-13,ee1cc492-9867-48d3-a612-c1fb491d2916,ca.m.1883,Mr. WOODSWORTH:,,THE BUDGET,CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL,FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE,I do not know anything that quite so clearly demonstrates that the banks, in the last analysis, as my hon. friend from Southeast Grey (Miss Macphail) suggests, are the government of this country. It is an astonishing state of affairs, and I am surprised that Conservative members will even attempt to justify that kind of thing. What I should like to ask is this, and possibly the Finance minister can tell us: Did the government of this country give guarantees to the banks. I am informed that the government gave to the banks guarantees similar in terms to those which they refused to the province of Manitoba. That is something which I think we are entitled to know in this house. In the meantime we have this governmental institution, the savings bank of the province of Manitoba, forced to go out of business. Further the federal government apparently, so far as anything to the contrary has yet been revealed, refused to give the assistance which might have saved the provincial savings bank.

Further than that, let me say that the banks are going outside of their own realm to such an extent that only the other day I had this resolution sent to me from the city clerk of the city of Winnipeg. I am not blaming the government for this situation, but I think it is well that the government and the country should know how far the banks are going and what resentment they are arousing even in official quarters in my part of Canada. This letter from the city olerk of the city of Winnipeg, dated March 30, 1932, reads as follows :
I beg to append a copy of resolution passed by the council of the city of Winnipeg this morning, namely:-
Whereas there appears to be a growing tendency for certain banks to engage in the purchase and sale of municipal securities;
And whereas owing to the relationship between municipalities and their bankers this
The Budget-Mr. Woodsworth
18 an undesirable and dangerous development which tends to place too much control in the hands of the banks, undermine their prestige and work to the disadvantage of the people as a whole;
Now therefore be it resolved that this council does protest against the present practice whereby certain banks purchase and sell municipal securities, even the securities of their own clients.

And it is further resolved that this council is of the opinion, and recommends, that this whole question be thoroughly investigated by the Dominion government before the time when amendments to the Bank Act are up for consideration in 1933; and further recommends that a thorough inquiry be made by parliament into all the circumstances relating to the connection of certain banks with the municipal and provincial bond and debenture issues which have been oifered to the public in recent months.
I pass that on from the city council of Winnipeg to the Minister of Finance urging that he make the investigation requested.

My colleague spoke with regard to the question of unemployment. I have not very much to add to what he said, but I would point this out, that we have no indication that the government is taking any steps adequate to meet the needs of the situation.

Might I offer a suggestion which was given to me and which I think has some merit, and that is with regard to single men, of whom we have so many in the west, men recruited very largely to do harvesting and construction work which was necessary in the earlier days. It is suggested that as an emergency measure-it is no permanent solution whatever, but it would be greatly preferable to the soup kitchen idea-that there be recruited a peace army; that every unemployed man be given a chance to earn $1.10 a day, with everything found, and that this peace army go into the north country to clear brush, to make highways and to beautify our parks and other areas, thus creating assets which would be of permanent value to us, especially so in view of the tourist business which has developed in Canada. More than anything else such an arrangement might help to save the morale of these men who are being degraded by hand-outs of food, and provision of very wretched shelter. I cannot see how any men with spirit in them can very long tolerate the kind of treatment single men are now receiving.

Further than that, I think of the families and their sufferings. In the outskirts of Winnipeg, forming part of my own constituency, is the little village of Brooklands. Recently^ survey was made in that village, and out of 600 families it was found that heads of 180 families were out of work. That situation is fairly typical of a very considerable portion of my constituency. When I was home at Easter I visited some of the homes in that section, and I should like to tell about one of them. In that home I found a man, a skilled mechanic, who has not had work for months. At the present time he is ill. His wife, a woman of rather exceptional ability, came from the old land, and has had good cultural opportunities. There are seven children. The city is supporting that family entirely, giving them groceries, milk, bread, fuhl, light and water. Further than that, it is making a small grant to the mortgage company, because in part the home is owned by the family, and in order that the mortgage should not be foreclosed and the people forced out on the street certain payments are being made to the mortgage company. Clothing has to be obtained in indirect ways. The worst feature however is this: In that home there were four big boys, out of school, sitting hour after hour, day after day, week after week, and month after month with absolutely nothing to do. Two of the older boys, since they were thirteen or fourteen years of age had helped on western farms, getting out as best they could and finding jobs. A few years ago that was possible, but to-day no such work is available. One of those boys told me he had been working in this haphazard way since he was thirteen years of age. and he was coming to realize that unless he soon learned a trade he could not make a success of life.

Thousands of boys are in precisely the same condition. I wish I could tell hon. members of this house about an exhibition I attended at Easter time showing work done by a group of unemployed boys. The finances of the department in charge however are at an end, and those boys are now on the street again with nothing to do. It seems to me a heavy responsibility rests upon some public body. As we say in our amendment, as this parliament is the body with the widest legislative power, it seems it is the responsibility of parliament definitely to lay plans to meet a need of this character. While I do not think the constructive suggestion we make in our amendment goes very far, it does seem to me it would cut down the debts, stabilize the dollar and help stimulate industrial activity that would tide us over for the time being. I urge upon hon. members that they must recognize the fact that we are in no temporary depression; we are facing the break-up of the system. That break-up may not come for a period of a few months or
Royal Assent
years or it may come quiekljr. We are not justified however in neglecting to face the seriousness of the situation.
On motion of Mr. Dickie the debate was adjourned.
